```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

markers <- data.frame(
  marker_a = c(4.1, 5.2, NA, 6.0),
  marker_b = c(12, 10, 9, 11),
  marker_c = rep(NA_real_, 4)
)
safe_mean <- function(x) {
  if (!is.numeric(x) || !is.null(dim(x))) {
    stop("x must be a numeric vector", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (any(is.infinite(x))) {
    stop("x must not contain infinite values", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (all(is.na(x))) return(NA_real_)
  mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
}
one_summary <- function(x) {
  m <- safe_mean(x)
  n <- sum(!is.na(x))
  c(n = n, mean = m, sd = if (n >= 2) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_)
}

# Synthetic teaching data for BIOS 6301. Not real patients.
set.seed(6301)
n <- 60
trial <- data.frame(
  id        = sprintf("P%03d", 1:n),
  arm       = rep(c("Placebo", "Treatment"), each = n / 2),
  site      = sample(1:4, n, replace = TRUE),
  age       = round(rnorm(n, 61, 9)),
  sex       = sample(c("F", "M"), n, replace = TRUE),
  weight_kg = round(rnorm(n, 82, 15), 1),
  sbp_0     = round(rnorm(n, 148, 14)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
trial$sbp_12 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 14, 8), rnorm(n, 3, 8)))

# Added for this session: a 6-week visit, so there are three outcome columns
# to iterate over and a three-column matrix for the apply() margins demo.
trial$sbp_6 <- round(trial$sbp_0 -
  ifelse(trial$arm == "Treatment", rnorm(n, 9, 7), rnorm(n, 2, 7)))

outcomes <- c("sbp_0", "sbp_6", "sbp_12")
sbp_mat  <- as.matrix(trial[, outcomes])
rownames(sbp_mat) <- trial$id

# The same extract, re-run a month later. Nothing about the query changed;
# site 3's most recent enrolments simply happen to all be female. This is the
# only difference between trial and trial_jun, and it is the whole sapply demo.
trial_jun <- trial
trial_jun$sex[trial_jun$site == 3] <- "F"

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 15))
```

# 1 · Doing the same thing many times {.section-divider}

## Repeat a function whose contract is already checked {.smaller}

Session 11 defined reusable operations; Session 12 checked their behavior.
Now repeat an operation over several inputs:

```r
summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_0)
summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_6)
summarise_by_arm(trial, sbp_12)
summarise_by_arm(trial, weight_kg)
summarise_by_arm(trial, age)
# ... and eight more outcomes in the final project
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The duplication did not disappear. It **moved up one level** — from the body of
the block to the list of calls.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
A function names *what* you are doing. Iteration names *what you are doing it
to*.
:::


## Ways to express repeated work {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.9em"}
| | Looks like | Gives you |
|---|---|---|
| **Loop** | `for (v in outcomes) { ... }` | Nothing. You manage the result yourself |
| **Apply family** | `lapply(outcomes, f)` | A list, one element per input |
| **`purrr`** | `map(outcomes, f)` | A list; typed variants require scalar results |
| **Vectorized** | `sqrt(x)`, `x > 140` | The answer, with no iteration written at all |
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The first three are the same idea with different bookkeeping. The fourth is a
direct expression of vector work. Prefer it when its behavior matches the task.
:::


# 2 · `for`, `while`, and pre-allocation {.section-divider}

## Anatomy of a `for` loop {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: for-anatomy
for (v in outcomes) {
  cat(v, ":", round(mean(trial[[v]]), 1), "mmHg\n")
}
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
- `v` takes each element of `outcomes` **in turn**. It is a real variable and it
  survives the loop.
- `trial[[v]]` — double brackets, because `v` holds a *name*, not a column.
- This loop **prints**. It does not produce an object. That is the next slide,
  and it is where the trouble is.
:::


## Store the results of a checked function {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: safe-marker-loop
marker_means <- setNames(numeric(ncol(markers)), names(markers))
for (j in seq_along(markers)) {
  marker_means[j] <- safe_mean(markers[[j]])
}
marker_means
```

`safe_mean()` is the helper from Sessions 11–12. It handles missingness and
validates each column. The loop chooses inputs and stores outputs.

**Practice:** explain `[[j]]` versus `[j]`, then predict the result for a
data frame with zero columns.

## Pre-allocate, do not grow {.smaller}

Same answer, two ways. Watch the clock.

```{r}
#| label: prealloc-bench
grow <- function(k) {
  out <- numeric(0)                                  # grows on every iteration
  for (i in seq_len(k)) out <- c(out, sqrt(i))
  out
}

prealloc <- function(k) {
  out <- numeric(k)                           # the right size, once
  for (i in seq_len(k)) out[i] <- sqrt(i)
  out
}

```

## Check equality before comparing elapsed time {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: prealloc-timing
stopifnot(identical(grow(20000), prealloc(20000)))
system.time(grow(20000))["elapsed"]
system.time(prealloc(20000))["elapsed"]
```


## Why growing is quadratic {.smaller}

`out <- c(out, x)` does not append. It **allocates a new vector and copies the
old one into it**, every single iteration.

```{r}
#| label: quadratic
#| echo: false
grow2 <- function(k) {
  out <- numeric(0)
  for (i in seq_len(k)) out <- c(out, sqrt(i))
  out
}
elapsed <- function(e) round(system.time(e)["elapsed"], 2)
data.frame(
  k       = c(5000, 10000, 20000),
  seconds = c(elapsed(grow2(5000)),
              elapsed(grow2(10000)),
              elapsed(grow2(20000)))
) |> kable()
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The copying work grows quadratically. Elapsed times also reflect allocation,
garbage collection, and measurement noise. Building a vector of length
`k` this way copies about `k²/2` values.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
`rbind()`-ing rows onto a data frame inside a loop is the same bug, and worse —
a data frame copy is far more expensive than a vector copy.
:::


## `seq_along()`, and the empty-vector trap {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: empty-trap
sbp <- numeric(0)          # a filter that matched nobody
1:length(sbp)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: empty-trap-loop
for (i in 1:length(sbp)) {
  cat("iteration", i, "gives value:", sbp[i], "\n")
}
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: empty-trap-fix
seq_along(sbp)             # the fix: length zero means zero iterations
```


## `while`: repeat while a condition is true {.smaller}

```r
while (condition) {
  # do one step
  # update the values used by condition
}
```

1. Check `condition` **before** the first step.
2. If `TRUE`, run the body and check the condition again.
3. If `FALSE`, skip the body and continue after the loop.

The condition must be one nonmissing logical value. The body may run **zero times**.
Update the state so the condition can become false; otherwise the loop may never end.

Use `for` to visit a supplied sequence. Use `while` when a condition determines
whether another step is needed.

## A bounded `while` loop, one step at a time {.smaller}

**Goal:** start at 1 and halve the value until it is below 0.01.

```{r}
#| label: while-halving
x <- 1
iteration <- 0L
max_iterations <- 100L
while (x >= 0.01 && iteration < max_iterations) {
  x <- x / 2
  iteration <- iteration + 1L
}
c(value = x, iterations = iteration)
```

The values are `1 → 0.5 → 0.25 → ... → 0.0078125`: **seven updates**.
`&&` requires both conditions to be true. The limit prevents endless iteration
if the target is not reached.

## Check why the loop stopped {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: while-stop-reason
reason <- if (x < 0.01) "threshold reached" else "iteration limit"
reason
```

Stopping is not proof of success: the iteration limit may have ended the loop.

**Predict, then rerun from the initialization:**

- Change `max_iterations` to `3L`: what value and stopping reason do you get?
- Start at `x <- 0.005`: how many times does the body run?
- Remove `x <- x / 2`: does the safeguard still stop the loop?

The next value depends on the previous value; this is a natural use of a loop.

# 3 · What "vectorized" actually means {.section-divider}

## The loop is still there. It is in C {.smaller}

```{mermaid}
%%| echo: false
%%| fig-width: 10.5
flowchart LR
  A["<b>sum(x)</b>"] --> B["<b>one</b> call<br/>into C"]
  B --> C["1,000,000<br/>additions,<br/>compiled"]
  D["<b>for (i in ...)</b><br/>s &lt;- s + x[i]"] --> E["<b>1,000,000</b> trips<br/>through the<br/>R interpreter"]
  E --> F["look up s,<br/>look up x, index,<br/>add, assign —<br/>every time"]
  style A fill:#CFAE70,stroke:#8a7448,color:#fff
  style D fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style C fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
  style F fill:#f4efe4,stroke:#CFAE70
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
A vectorized interface accepts a whole vector. Common primitives such as
`sum()` perform their internal loop in compiled code; not every vector-shaped interface does.
:::


## Compare three implementations on the same input {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: bench-three
y  <- rnorm(5e5)
tt <- \(expr) system.time(expr)[["elapsed"]]      # seconds, unnamed

c(`for loop`   = tt({
                   out <- numeric(length(y))
                   for (i in seq_along(y)) out[i] <- y[i]^2
                 }),
  `vapply()`   = tt(vapply(y, \(v) v^2, numeric(1))),
  `vectorized` = tt(y^2))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
These are local measurements, not universal speed rankings. A functional still
calls an R function per element. Check results, repeat timings, and report input size.
:::


## The vectorized answers you already have {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.84em"}
| Instead of looping to... | Write |
|---|---|
| build a new column from an old one | `trial$high <- trial$sbp_0 > 140` |
| choose per row | `ifelse()`, `if_else()`, `case_when()` |
| total or average a column | `sum()`, `mean()`, `cumsum()` |
| average across visits, per patient | `rowMeans()`, `rowSums()` |
| average one visit, across patients | `colMeans()`, `colSums()` |
| element-wise max of two vectors | `pmax()`, `pmin()` |
| count each value | `table()` |
| test membership | `x %in% y` |
| find where a condition holds | `which()` |
| running total | `cumsum()`, `cumprod()`, `cummax()` |
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Before writing a loop, check whether a function already expresses the operation
and has the missing-value behavior you need.
:::


# 4 · The apply family {.section-divider}

## `apply()`: margins on a matrix {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: apply-rows
# MARGIN = 1: one answer per ROW
head(apply(sbp_mat, 1, max), 4)
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: apply-cols
# MARGIN = 2: one answer per COLUMN
round(apply(sbp_mat, 2, mean), 1)
```
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
`sbp_mat` is 60 × 3: one row per patient, one column per visit. **`MARGIN` is
the dimension you keep.**
:::

. . .

```r
# and when the function is mean or sum, do not use apply() at all
rowMeans(sbp_mat)  # one mean per patient
colMeans(sbp_mat)  # one mean per visit
```


## `apply()` on a data frame: the coercion trap {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: apply-coerce
apply(trial[, c("id", "sbp_0", "sbp_12")], 1, max) |> head(4)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Those are patient **IDs**, not blood pressures. `apply()` needs a matrix, so it
called `as.matrix()` — and a matrix holds one type, so every number became
`"P001"`-style text.
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
Session 3's coercion rules, arriving through a new door. `apply()` on a data
frame with any character column silently converts **everything** to character.
:::


## `lapply()`: a list in, a list out {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: lapply-demo
summary_of <- function(x) {
  round(c(n = sum(!is.na(x)), mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)), 1)
}

results <- lapply(trial[outcomes], summary_of)
results
```


## One result can contain several statistics {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: one-summary
one_summary <- function(x) {
  m <- safe_mean(x)
  n <- sum(!is.na(x))
  c(n = n, mean = m,
    sd = if (n >= 2) sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) else NA_real_)
}
one_summary(markers$marker_a)
```

## Apply the multivalue summary to every marker {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: one-summary-list
lapply(markers, one_summary)
```

The result of one call is a named numeric vector of length three. The result
of `lapply()` is a list containing one such vector per marker.

## `sapply()`: convenience, and what it costs {.smaller}

`sapply()` is `lapply()` plus a guess about what shape you wanted.

```{r}
#| label: sapply-good
sapply(trial[outcomes], summary_of)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: sapply-sex
# For each site, which sexes are enrolled?
sapply(split(trial$sex, trial$site), unique)
```


## The day the data changed {.smaller}

Same code. Same query. The extract re-run a month later:

```{r}
#| label: sapply-bad
sapply(split(trial_jun$sex, trial_jun$site), unique)
```

## The same call can return a different type {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: sapply-bad-class
class(sapply(split(trial$sex,     trial$site), unique))
class(sapply(split(trial_jun$sex, trial_jun$site), unique))
```

. . .

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
A matrix on Tuesday, a list on Wednesday. Nothing downstream was written to
handle both.
:::


## `vapply()`: declare the shape {.smaller}

`FUN.VALUE` is a template. It says what one answer looks like.

```{r}
#| label: vapply-good
vapply(trial[outcomes], summary_of, numeric(3))
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: vapply-error
#| error: true
vapply(split(trial_jun$sex, trial_jun$site), unique, character(2))
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
The error names the element that broke the contract: `FUN(X[[3]])`. That is
site 3.
:::


## Match the output template to the operation {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: summary-template
template <- c(n = 0, mean = 0, sd = 0)
summary_matrix <- vapply(markers, one_summary, template)
summary_matrix
```

One statistic per marker: use `numeric(1)`.
Three statistics per marker: use a length-three template or `lapply()`.

**Practice:** predict the dimensions for zero marker columns. Why would
`vapply(markers, one_summary, numeric(1))` fail?

## Input checks and output checks do different jobs {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: typed-input-guard
#| error: true
bad <- list(good = c(2, 4), broken = "not numeric")
vapply(bad, safe_mean, numeric(1))
```

`safe_mean()` rejects the invalid **input**. `vapply()` checks each **output**.
It does not validate inputs for the function you supply.

`mean("not numeric")` warns and returns numeric `NA`. That result can satisfy
a numeric output template, even though the input is wrong.

## `tapply()`: split, apply, combine {.smaller}

You met this in session 4. Look at it again as a **functional**:

```{r}
#| label: tapply-demo
round(tapply(trial$sbp_12, trial$arm, mean), 1)
```

. . .

```{r}
#| label: tapply-two
round(tapply(trial$sbp_12, list(trial$arm, trial$site), mean), 1)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
```r
# the tidyverse way
trial |> group_by(arm) |> summarise(mean = mean(sbp_12))
```
:::


## The family on one slide {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.82em"}
| Function | Input | Output | Use it |
|---|---|---|---|
| `apply(m, MARGIN, f)` | array or matrix | simplified array, vector, or list | Rows or columns of a matrix |
| `lapply(x, f)` | vector or list | **always a list** | The safe default |
| `sapply(x, f)` | vector or list | vector, matrix, *or list* | Console only |
| `vapply(x, f, FUN.VALUE)` | vector or list | the shape you declared | **In scripts** |
| `tapply(x, g, f)` | vector + grouping | vector or matrix | Grouped summary |
:::


# 5 · Head to head: base and `purrr` {.section-divider}

## Meet the `purrr` package {.smaller}

`purrr` is a tidyverse package for applying a function repeatedly to elements
of a vector or list. It offers a consistent interface and named output types.

```r
# Install once in the Console if needed:
install.packages("purrr")

# Load in each new R session:
library(purrr)
```

- `map(x, f)` applies `f` to each element of `x` and returns a list.
- `map_dbl(x, f)` returns one number per element as a double vector.
- Put the data first and the function second, as in `lapply(x, f)`.

Next, compare the same calculation using base R and `purrr`.


## Base R and `purrr` list mappings {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
### base R

```{r}
#| label: hh-lapply
res <- lapply(trial[outcomes],
              summary_of)
res$sbp_12
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
### `purrr`

```r
library(purrr)

res <- map(trial[outcomes],
           summary_of)
res$sbp_12
```
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
Both `lapply()` and `map()` take data first and return a list. The typed
`purrr` variants make scalar output contracts explicit in the function name.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
The base R route is sufficient for the lab. Use the `purrr` alternatives if
the package is installed; compare their results with the base implementation.
:::


## Typed variants: `map_dbl()` and friends {.smaller}

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
### base R

```{r}
#| label: hh-vapply
vapply(trial[outcomes],
       mean, numeric(1))
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
### `purrr`

```r
map_dbl(trial[outcomes], mean)
```
:::
:::

. . .

::: {style="font-size:0.86em"}
| Want back | base R | `purrr` |
|---|---|---|
| a list | `lapply(x, f)` | `map(x, f)` |
| a double vector | `vapply(x, f, numeric(1))` | `map_dbl(x, f)` |
| a character vector | `vapply(x, f, character(1))` | `map_chr(x, f)` |
| a logical vector | `vapply(x, f, logical(1))` | `map_lgl(x, f)` |
| an integer vector | `vapply(x, f, integer(1))` | `map_int(x, f)` |
| a data frame of rows | `do.call(rbind, lapply(...))` | `list_rbind(map(x, f))` |
:::


## Anonymous functions and extra arguments {.smaller}

`\(x)` is shorthand for `function(x)`. Use it when a small wrapper does not
need a separate name.

```{r}
#| label: lambda-base
vapply(trial[outcomes], \(x) round(mean(x), digits = 1), numeric(1))
```

```r
# The corresponding purrr call
purrr::map_dbl(trial[outcomes], \(x) round(mean(x), digits = 1))
```

The wrapper receives one column and returns one number. If it returns several
statistics, choose a list or a matrix template instead.

## The same job, twice {.smaller}

**Task.** For every outcome, the treatment-minus-placebo difference in means.

::: columns
::: {.column width="49%"}
```{r}
#| label: hh-base-final
vapply(outcomes, \(v) {
  m <- tapply(trial[[v]],
              trial$arm, mean)
  round(m[["Treatment"]] -
        m[["Placebo"]], 1)
}, numeric(1))
```
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
```r
map_dbl(outcomes, \(v) {
  trial |>
    group_by(arm) |>
    summarise(m = mean(.data[[v]])) |>
    pull(m) |>
    diff() |>
    round(1)
}) |> set_names(outcomes)
```
:::
:::

. . .

::: {.smaller}
For this unnamed character input, `vapply()` uses the strings as output names;
`map_dbl()` preserves existing names, so we set names explicitly here. And `v` holds a **string**, so it is `.data[[v]]` — not last
week's curly-curly, which wants a bare column name.
:::


# 6 · Choosing, and when a loop is right {.section-divider}

## Which one do I want? {.smaller}

::: {style="font-size:0.88em"}
| If... | Use |
|---|---|
| A vectorized function matches the contract | Prefer its direct expression of the task |
| One value per element, type known | `vapply()` / `map_dbl()` |
| Results have different shapes | `lapply()` / `map()` |
| You are looping for a side effect | `for` loop, or `walk()` |
| Step *i* depends on step *i−1* | An explicit loop; accumulation tools are another option |
| You are exploring at the console | Whatever is quickest to type |
:::

. . .

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
Prefer clear code that satisfies the contract. Measure representative work
before deciding that performance justifies a more complex implementation.
:::


## A loop with a dependency between steps {.smaller}

**Iterative dependence**: step *i* needs the result of step *i−1*.

```{r}
#| label: newton-mle
# Newton-Raphson. Each step is computed FROM the previous estimate.
x     <- 1
trace <- numeric(4)

for (i in seq_len(4)) {
  x        <- x - (x^2 - 2) / (2 * x)
  trace[i] <- x
}

round(trace, 8)
```

. . .

::: {.smaller}
An independent mapping is not the right model: iteration 3 uses the state
created by iteration 2. An explicit loop makes that dependency visible. **MCMC, EM, gradient descent, and every iterative
optimiser have this shape.**
:::


## Accumulating results without growing {.smaller}

The pattern for "one row of results per iteration":

```{r}
#| label: accumulate
#| results: hold
res <- vector("list", length(outcomes))     # pre-allocated LIST
names(res) <- outcomes

for (v in outcomes) {
  res[[v]] <- data.frame(
    outcome = v,
    mean    = round(mean(trial[[v]]), 1),
    sd      = round(sd(trial[[v]]), 1)
  )
}

do.call(rbind, res)                          # combine ONCE, at the end
```


# 7 · Verify, measure, and practice {.section-divider}

## Equivalence comes before speed {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: equivalence-first
row_loop <- function(m) {
  out <- numeric(nrow(m))
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(m))) out[i] <- mean(m[i, ])
  names(out) <- rownames(m)
  out
}
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(row_loop(sbp_mat), rowMeans(sbp_mat))))
```

Check values, missing-value policy, names, types, and dimensions. Two fast
implementations of different calculations are not interchangeable.

## Measure representative work repeatedly {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: repeated-timing
bench_input <- matrix(seq_len(20000) / 100, nrow = 1000)
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(row_loop(bench_input), rowMeans(bench_input))))
invisible(row_loop(bench_input))  # warm up before recording
invisible(rowMeans(bench_input))
timings <- matrix(NA_real_, 5, 2,
                  dimnames = list(NULL, c("loop", "rowMeans")))
for (k in seq_len(nrow(timings))) {
  timings[k, "loop"] <- system.time(row_loop(bench_input))[["elapsed"]]
  timings[k, "rowMeans"] <- system.time(rowMeans(bench_input))[["elapsed"]]
}
```

## Read and report repeated timings {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: repeated-timing-results
timings
```

Report dimensions, repetitions, R version, and variability. A displayed zero
can mean the task is below the timer's resolution, not that it costs no time.

## Memory and the final recommendation {.smaller}

```{r}
#| label: memory-size
object.size(bench_input)
object.size(rowMeans(bench_input))
```

`object.size()` estimates an R object's stored size. It does not measure peak
memory or all temporary allocations during a calculation.

Recommend an implementation using correctness, stable shape, readability,
and measured time. State when you would reconsider the choice.

## Lab route and exit check {.smaller}

| Task | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| Preallocated loop | One named mean per marker |
| Matrix apply and rowMeans | Matching participant means |
| lapply and vapply | Explain list versus numeric output |
| One supplied benchmark | Interpret repeated timings |

**Exit check:** choose a tool for a scalar result, a list of results, and a
step that depends on the previous output. Optional: repeat with purrr.

Use `map()` followed by `list_rbind()` for a current purrr row-binding workflow.
The older `map_dfr()` interface is superseded.

## Summary {.smaller}

- Vectorize when the vector expression states the operation directly.
- Use a loop when the algorithm has state or the steps need to remain explicit.
- Preallocate output; repeated growth is the expensive pattern.
- Prefer functionals with a stable output contract for repeated independent work.
- Verify equivalence before benchmarking or optimizing.
